strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and non-trivial extension of Mean Field Games to the partially observable, common-noise setting (POMFG-CN), with a careful formalization showing why naive history-dependence is intractable (Ht growing exponentially) and identifying the special case of shared observations that restores tractability of the analytic mean-field update — this is a genuine conceptual contribution.

RSPG is the first Hybrid Structural Method that supports history-aware, non-tabular policies with continuous observations, extending prior work (SPG/Yang et al. 2025) that was restricted to memoryless tabular policies; the architecture (RNN over shared observations only, independent of individual state) is a sensible design that preserves the computational complexity of the analytic mean-field update.

MFAX is a solid engineering contribution: it cleanly separates white-box/black-box transition access, uses functional (non-materialized) matrix representations to reduce memory from O(|S|^2) to O(|S|+|S||A|+|Z|), and demonstrates substantial (10x-1000x) speedups over OpenSpiel/MFGLib on a standard benchmark, which is useful to the community.

Empirical evaluation spans three environments (two adapted standard MFG benchmarks plus a novel macroeconomics environment with heterogeneous agents, common noise, and partial observability, solved for the first time in this form), compares against multiple relevant baselines (SPG, IPPO, RIPPO, M-OMD), and includes both quantitative (exploitability vs wall-clock time) and qualitative (visualized anticipatory behavior) analyses.

Good reproducibility support: detailed pseudocode (Algorithms 1-4), exhaustive hyperparameter tables and sweep ranges, environment specifications with all parameters, and an ablation isolating the effect of the ordinal (ordinality-preserving) action parameterization versus plain categorical policies.
weaknesses: No formal convergence guarantees or theoretical analysis are provided for RSPG (e.g., convergence to a mean-field Nash equilibrium, bias/variance characterization of the gradient estimator); the contribution is empirical/algorithmic rather than accompanied by theory, despite the paper's heavy formalism in Sections 2-5.

The tractability result is restricted to the special case where observations are a deterministic/shared function of (mu_t, z_t) and policies only condition on this shared history — individual-state-dependent observations (the more general and arguably more realistic POMFG-CN case introduced in Section 5) remain intractable and unaddressed algorithmically, somewhat narrowing the practical scope of the claimed 'first history-aware HSM' contribution.

The exploitability metric used for evaluation is computed against a common, more expressive best-response class with full information rather than each algorithm's true information set, which the authors acknowledge renders it more like a conservative upper bound/regret proxy rather than a principled equilibrium-distance measure; this weakens the strength of 'state-of-the-art performance' claims.

Empirical validation is limited to three environments (two are close variants of standard toy MFG benchmarks, one macroeconomic case study), with results averaged over only 10 seeds; there is no evaluation on larger/higher-dimensional state spaces to demonstrate scalability limits of the discretization-dependent analytic mean-field update, which the paper's own related-work discussion notes as a general weakness of HSMs versus RL.

The 'unified taxonomy' contribution (Section 3) is largely expository/organizational rather than technically novel, and the Impact Statement is boilerplate despite the paper explicitly targeting a macroeconomic policy application (interest rates, wages, consumption) where downstream societal implications could be more substantively discussed.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy (e.g., Sections 2-5 rely on many overloaded symbols and matrix operators), which may hinder accessibility; several central claims (e.g., 'order-of-magnitude faster convergence') are supported only by visual inspection of Figure 2 without corresponding quantitative summary tables of time-to-threshold-exploitability.

strengths: Provides a clear, somewhat pedagogically useful unified taxonomy of DP, RL, and Hybrid Structural Methods for MFGs, and a careful formalization of Partially Observable MFGs with Common Noise (POMFG-CN), including an explicit characterization of when the analytic mean-field update remains tractable under partial observability.

RSPG is a reasonable and technically sound extension of SPG to history-aware (recurrent) policies in the 'shared observation' special case, exploiting known individual dynamics for lower-variance structural gradients while keeping the exact mean-field update tractable.

MFAX engineering contribution is solid and practically useful: functional (non-materialized) representation of the mean-field transition operator gives large wall-clock speedups over OpenSpiel/MFGLib, and the library explicitly separates white-box/black-box dynamics and supports common noise, partial observability, and multiple initial distributions, which existing libraries lack.

Experiments span three environments of increasing realism (Linear Quadratic, Beach Bar, and a Krusell-Smith-style heterogeneous-agent macroeconomics model), and qualitative visualizations (anticipatory wealth spend-down, bar-avoidance before closure) give intuitive, convincing evidence that history-aware policies capture more realistic behavior than memoryless ones.

Reproducibility materials are thorough: full environment definitions, hyperparameter tables, sweep ranges, algorithm pseudocode, and compute details are provided in the appendix, and code/library release is promised.
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution is narrower than advertised: tractability is only achieved by restricting to the special case where the shared observation is a deterministic function of the aggregate state and the policy conditions only on the observation history. This essentially converts the problem back into an augmented fully-observable-style MFG via a history sufficient statistic, a standard idea in POMDP literature; the truly hard general case (observations depending on individual state) is explicitly acknowledged as intractable and left unsolved, so the claimed generality of 'POMFG-CN' is undercut by the fact that only a fairly restrictive subclass is actually handled algorithmically.

The exploitability metric used for evaluation is a non-standard, self-admitted approximation that 'resembles regret' rather than true exploitability, computed against a common, more expressive best-response class with perfect information; this ad hoc choice, while pragmatically justified, makes cross-algorithm comparisons less rigorous and could differentially bias comparisons between memoryless and history-aware methods.

Empirical support for the central claims is somewhat thin: only three environments (two small toy MFGs and one macro model), 10 seeds with visibly wide confidence intervals in Figure 2, and all RL baselines (IPPO, RIPPO, M-OMD) are the authors' own reimplementations rather than externally validated baselines, making 'state-of-the-art performance' claims difficult to fully trust.

In the macroeconomics environment, SPG (memoryless) and RSPG achieve similar exploitability, undercutting the paper's main quantitative claim that history-awareness improves convergence to equilibrium; the advantage is argued qualitatively (anticipatory behavior) rather than through the primary quantitative metric, weakening the overall empirical narrative.

The method fundamentally requires known, white-box individual transition dynamics and discretized/tractable state-action spaces, which is a strong assumption limiting applicability beyond simulation-based or structurally known environments; this limitation is somewhat underplayed relative to the strength of the 'state-of-the-art' and 'first-time solved' claims.

No theoretical convergence or equilibrium guarantees are provided for RSPG (unlike some cited competing methods with monotonicity-based guarantees), and the choice to stop gradients through mean-field transitions in Algorithm 1 is not theoretically justified or analyzed for bias.

The Impact Statement is generic boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with the fact that the macroeconomics application domain (policy-relevant heterogeneous-agent modeling) could have downstream societal implications worth discussing.

strengths: Clear and useful theoretical contribution: the paper formalizes Partially Observable Mean Field Games with Common Noise (POMFGs-CN) and carefully identifies the special case of shared aggregate observations under which the analytic mean-field update remains tractable despite history-dependent policies — this is a non-trivial technical insight that resolves an exponential blow-up (IAOH growth) present in the general formulation.
The unified taxonomy of DP, RL, and HSM approaches (Section 3, Information Boxes 1-3) is a valuable organizing contribution that clarifies the literature and situates the proposed method precisely.

RSPG is a reasonable and well-motivated algorithmic extension of prior memoryless HSMs (SPG) to history-aware policies, with a sensible architecture (RNN decoupled from individual state) that preserves the asymptotic cost of the analytic mean-field update.

The experimental evaluation covers three distinct environments (including a nontrivial macroeconomics heterogeneous-agent model), reports wall-clock comparisons against multiple RL baselines (IPPO, RIPPO, M-OMD) and an ablation (SPG), and includes qualitative visualizations showing anticipatory behavior only emerges with history-aware policies — this strengthens the claim that history-awareness matters practically, not just in principle.

MFAX is a genuine systems contribution with concrete, reproducible speed benchmarks (10x–1000x faster mean-field updates than OpenSpiel/MFGLib) and support for features (partial observability, common noise, multiple initial distributions, white-box/black-box distinction) missing from existing libraries; code/implementation details and hyperparameter sweeps are documented extensively in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.

The continuous-action parameterization trick (evaluating log-densities at fixed intervals to preserve ordinality) is a nice, empirically validated design choice (Appendix C.4.1) that meaningfully improves performance over naive categorical parameterization.
weaknesses: The exploitability metric used for evaluation is non-standard: best responses are computed over a common, more expressive policy class with full information, regardless of whether the learned policy is memoryless or history-aware. While the authors acknowledge this makes the metric 'resemble regret' rather than true exploitability, it is unclear whether this choice systematically favors history-aware methods (like RSPG) in the reported comparisons, since the best-response benchmark itself has access to information the evaluated policy does not use.

No convergence guarantees or theoretical analysis of RSPG are provided (unlike some RL-based MFG algorithms cited, e.g., M-OMD variants with monotonicity-based guarantees); the contribution is purely algorithmic/empirical, which somewhat limits the theoretical significance relative to its claims of being 'state-of-the-art.'

The empirical validation, while spanning three environments, relies on small-to-moderate discrete/discretized state-action spaces (100–1000 states); because HSMs fundamentally require tractable, discretizable individual dynamics and analytic mean-field updates, the scalability of RSPG to larger or more complex state spaces (continuous high-dimensional states, dense transition kernels) is not empirically demonstrated, despite this being acknowledged as a limitation of HSMs generally.

Statistical reporting is somewhat thin: results are averaged over only 10 seeds with 95% CI bands shown in figures, but no formal significance testing, and the hyperparameter sweep selection criterion ('configurations that achieve both low exploitability and fast convergence') is subjective and could bias comparisons in favor of the proposed method.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate ('none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted'), providing no substantive discussion of potential societal implications, despite the paper explicitly targeting high-stakes application domains like macroeconomic policy and financial markets where model misuse or over-reliance on learned equilibria could have real consequences.

Several claims of novelty ('the first history-aware HSM,' 'solves for the first time') are asserted somewhat strongly; while the related work section is reasonably thorough, a more explicit discussion of exactly how the shared-observation assumption may or may not hold in the motivating real-world examples (e.g., whether financial market agents truly share identical information histories) would strengthen the practical significance claims.

strengths: Clear identification of a genuine methodological gap: existing Hybrid Structural Methods (HSMs) for MFGs are restricted to memoryless, tabular policies, and this paper is the first to extend HSMs to history-aware policies under partial observability with common noise.

The key technical insight—restricting memory to the history of shared public observations rather than the full individual-action-observation history—is elegant and practically important, since it keeps the mean-field a distribution over the (fixed) state space rather than an exponentially growing history space, preserving the tractability that makes HSMs attractive.

The paper is intellectually honest about the limits of its central assumption: Appendix A provides an explicit counter-example showing Assumption 6.1 does not hold in general, which is a commendable and rare level of rigor/self-scrutiny.
The unified taxonomy of DP/RL/HSM methods (Section 4, Information Boxes 1-3) is a genuinely useful pedagogical and organizational contribution to a fragmented literature.

Solid engineering contribution via MFAX: functional (rather than materialized-matrix) computation of mean-field updates, support for white-box/black-box duality, partial observability, common noise, and multiple initial distributions, with demonstrated large wall-clock speedups (10x–1000x) over existing libraries (Table 2), plus released code.

Empirical evaluation spans three qualitatively distinct environments (Linear Quadratic, Beach Bar, Macroeconomics) and includes reasonable hyperparameter sweeps, ablations (e.g., ordinal vs categorical action parameterization), and confidence intervals over 10 seeds, supporting reproducibility.

Results are consistent with the paper's central claims: RSPG matches SPG's fast convergence while learning demonstrably more realistic anticipatory behavior (visualized clearly in Figures 3, 4, 8), and both HSMs are shown to converge roughly an order of magnitude faster than RL baselines.
weaknesses: No formal convergence or equilibrium guarantees are provided for RSPG; the paper's own DP/HSM framing emphasizes exactness/structure, yet the core contribution lacks theoretical convergence analysis, leaving the equilibrium properties of the proposed method largely unverified beyond empirical stability.

The soundness of restricting policies to (s_t, o_{0:t}) rests on Assumption 6.1, which the authors themselves show is not generally valid (Appendix A); the paper offers only informal application-specific justification (financial/epidemiological examples) for why this approximation should be reasonable in the tested environments, without a way to quantify the resulting suboptimality.

Empirical validation is limited to three environments (two synthetic toy MFG benchmarks and one macroeconomic model), all relatively small-scale (|S| up to ~1000, discretized action spaces); it is unclear how RSPG scales with longer/more complex observation histories, larger state-action spaces, or richer partial-observability structures.

The exploitability metric used for comparison evaluates against a larger perfect-information policy class ΠPI as a conservative upper bound rather than the actual admissible (memory-restricted) policy class, which the authors acknowledge makes it a regret-like bound rather than an exact distance to the relevant Nash equilibrium — this weakens the strength of the equilibrium-quality claims.

The algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: RSPG is essentially SPG with a GRU-based observation-history encoder bolted on; the main contribution is more architectural/insight-based than a new learning principle, which may limit its perceived significance despite being useful.

Variance-reduction/scalability trade-offs specific to the recurrent extension (e.g., how gradient variance or wall-clock cost changes with history length, number of GRU layers, or larger hidden dimensions) are not systematically studied, despite variance reduction being the central selling point of HSMs.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored intersection of problems (common noise + partial observability + structural/variance-reduced learning) in MFGs, which the related-work section convincingly shows has not been jointly tackled before.
The DP/RL/HSM taxonomy (Information Boxes 1-3) is a clear and pedagogically useful organizing contribution that is currently missing from the MFG literature.

The authors are commendably transparent about the limits of their core approximation: Assumption 6.1 is explicitly flagged as an approximation rather than a general truth, and a concrete counter-example (Appendix A) is provided showing when it fails and is payoff-relevant. This kind of self-critical honesty is a positive rather than a weakness.

MFAX provides measurable practical value (10x-1000x faster mean-field updates vs. OpenSpiel/MFGLib in Table 2), functional (non-materialized) transition representations, and support for features (common noise, partial observability, multiple initial distributions) absent from prior libraries, which could be useful infrastructure for the community.

Reasonably thorough experimental protocol with multiple baselines (SPG, IPPO, RIPPO, M-OMD), 10 seeds with confidence intervals, an ablation on policy parameterization (ordinal vs. categorical), and qualitative visualizations (heatmaps, policy maps) that illustrate the intended behavioral phenomenon (anticipatory behavior).
weaknesses: No theoretical guarantee that RSPG converges to (or even approaches) a mean-field Nash equilibrium; the paper explicitly concedes this and notes that existing guarantees for related settings require assumptions (full observability, monotonicity, continuity) that do not hold here. For a paper whose central object is a Nash-equilibrium-seeking algorithm, this is a substantive soundness gap rather than a minor limitation.

The validity of restricting policies to condition only on (s_t, o_{0:t}) hinges on Assumption 6.1, which the authors themselves show can fail in a simple, payoff-relevant example. This means the policy class searched by RSPG may not contain the true equilibrium policy in general, undermining the claim that RSPG finds 'more behaviourally-realistic equilibria' rather than merely a reasonable heuristic restriction.

The exploitability metric used for comparison is explicitly described as 'a conservative regret-like upper bound rather than an exact distance to equilibrium,' evaluated against a larger perfect-information policy class ΠPI. Because this evaluation class differs structurally from the training policy class of memoryless baselines (SPG, IPPO, M-OMD), the reported exploitability gap between RSPG and these methods may partly reflect this structural mismatch rather than a genuine equilibrium-quality advantage; this confound is not controlled for or quantified.

Empirical validation is confined to three relatively small/stylized environments (|S| up to ~1000, low-dimensional common noise), all variants of standard toy MFG benchmarks; there is no evaluation at larger or more realistic scale, nor any environment where the sufficiency assumption is known to be violated, which would stress-test the practical robustness of the core approximation.

The core technical contribution (adding a GRU over public observations, broadcast across states, within the existing SPG/HSM gradient-computation machinery) is incremental relative to prior HSM work (SPG); much of the novelty is concentrated in problem formalization rather than algorithmic innovation.

The 'order-of-magnitude faster convergence' claim over RL baselines is somewhat expected given that HSMs assume white-box access to transition dynamics that RL methods deliberately forgo; this inherent informational asymmetry is not sufficiently discussed as a caveat to the speed comparison.

The abstract references a code/framework link that is blank/missing in the provided manuscript text, raising a minor but visible reproducibility/presentation concern, despite detailed hyperparameter tables in the appendix.

strengths: Addresses a clear and previously unaddressed gap: extending Hybrid Structural Methods (HSMs) to partially observable Mean Field Games with common noise, which is a natural and important generalization given many real applications (finance, epidemiology, communication networks) involve partial/public observability.

The paper is methodologically careful: it introduces a precise taxonomy of DP/RL/HSM methods, clearly identifies the tractability issue caused by the exponentially growing history space under partial observability, and proposes a principled restriction (Assumption 6.1) to shared public-observation histories to retain tractability.

Commendable intellectual honesty: the authors explicitly acknowledge that the sufficiency assumption (6.1) does not hold in general and provide an explicit counter-example in Appendix A demonstrating cases where it is violated and leads to suboptimality, which strengthens trust in the work's claims rather than overselling them.

Solid empirical evaluation across three qualitatively different environments (Linear Quadratic, Beach Bar, Macroeconomics), including visualizations of learned vs. best-response policies and mean-field evolution, showing that RSPG learns history-/anticipatory-aware behaviour (e.g., agents moving away from the bar before closure, or depleting wealth near the end of a finite horizon) that memoryless HSMs cannot capture.

The introduction of MFAX as an open JAX-based MFG framework is a useful infrastructural contribution, with substantial speed improvements over existing libraries (OpenSpiel, MFGLib) due to functional/sparse matrix-vector product implementations, and support for analytic/sample-based mean-field updates, common noise, and partial observability simultaneously -- a combination not available elsewhere.
Reasonably thorough ablations (e.g., ordinal vs categorical action parameterisation) and reporting of hyperparameter sweep details, improving reproducibility.

Honest discussion of limitations, in particular the lack of convergence guarantees to a Nash equilibrium, with appropriate justification as to why extending existing theoretical results is non-trivial.
weaknesses: The core exploitability metric used for comparison is only an upper bound (computed with respect to a larger perfect-information policy class ΠPI for fairness across memoryless and history-aware methods) rather than a true measure of distance to a Nash equilibrium within the admissible class, which somewhat weakens the strength of claims regarding 'proximity to equilibrium' for different methods, particularly for comparing RSPG against SPG/RL baselines that have different policy classes.

Experimental environments, while varied, remain relatively low/moderate-dimensional (discretized states up to ~1000, 1D/2D state spaces); it is unclear how RSPG's recurrent structural approach scales to larger or continuous individual state spaces where exact analytic mean-field updates become increasingly costly or infeasible, an issue the authors themselves flag as future work.

Hyperparameter sweep budgets differ substantially across methods (3 configurations for SPG/RSPG vs up to 243 for M-OMD), which, though explained, could raise concerns about whether the RL baselines (especially M-OMD, a strong baseline in the literature) are being presented under comparably optimized conditions.

The theoretical contribution is primarily an assumption-based restriction (public-observation memory) rather than a new convergence result; no formal guarantees are given that RSPG converges to an approximate Nash equilibrium even under Assumptions 1.1 and 6.1, leaving the theoretical grounding comparatively modest relative to the empirical contribution.

Applicability is restricted to settings with a shared/public observation channel (Assumption 1.1); many partially observable MFG settings of interest involve individual/private noisy observations of the aggregate state, which are explicitly outside the scope of this work and left for future extensions.

Wall-clock comparisons between MFAX (JAX, GPU) and other libraries (OpenSpiel in C++, MFGLib in Python, presumably CPU-bound) are influenced by implementation/hardware differences and may not isolate the algorithmic/method contribution versus engineering optimizations.
